title: The Labourer Whose Limbs Stopped Obeying Her — Backache, Ascending Weakness, and a Diagnosis Still Open

sections.heading: The Patient's Story
sections.content:
She is 50 years old and works as a labourer. Two months before coming to the hospital, she was entirely well. Then backache set in, sudden and gradually worsening, and she went to a local hospital where it settled with medication. It returned 20 days before this admission, this time not responding to what she took for it.

Ten days before admission, weakness began — sudden in onset, then marching upward through her body in a distinct order: first the lower limbs closer to her trunk, then the lower limbs further out, then the upper limbs closer to her trunk, then, oddly, the lower limbs again. In practical terms, everyday movements became difficult one by one: combing her hair, bringing food to her mouth, buttoning and unbuttoning her clothes, squatting and getting up from a squat, climbing stairs, putting on sandals, lifting her head off the pillow, even rolling over or getting up from bed. Her toes tripped when she walked. She had no trouble breathing, and her weakness didn't notably vary through the day — but an injection of tramadol brought her a couple of hours of relief each time.

She has no known diabetes, hypertension, tuberculosis, asthma, epilepsy, coronary disease, or stroke. In 2009 she had a hysterectomy with removal of both ovaries and tubes, done under spinal anesthesia for abnormal uterine bleeding.

sections.heading: What the Work-Up Showed So Far
sections.content:
- General exam: no pallor, icterus, cyanosis, clubbing, lymphadenopathy, or pedal edema
- Vitals: temperature 99°F, blood pressure 110/80 mmHg, pulse 78 bpm, respiratory rate 30/min, oxygen saturation 98% on room air, capillary glucose 100 mg/dL
- Neurological exam: conscious, oriented, cooperative; cranial nerves intact; motor power reduced symmetrically to 4-/5 in both upper and lower limbs (normal tone), with full hand grip strength; deep tendon and superficial reflexes preserved and symmetric, plantar responses flexor bilaterally; cerebellar, sensory, and autonomic examinations normal; spine non-tender; no meningeal signs
- Cardiorespiratory and abdominal exam: unremarkable
- Investigations sent: complete blood picture, urine examination, arterial blood gas, liver and renal function tests, thyroid profile, serology, random blood sugar, chest X-ray, X-ray of the sacroiliac joints, ECG, ultrasound of the abdomen and neck, MRI brain, and MRI of the cervical spine with whole-spine screening

sections.heading: How the Story Unfolded on the Ward
sections.content:
Her working diagnosis was framed broadly: quadriparesis under evaluation, with possibilities including a myopathy or a lytic bony (vertebral) lesion, multiple myeloma among the considerations. She was started on supportive treatment — B-complex injections, a muscle relaxant, an anti-emetic, a proton pump inhibitor, and tramadol for pain, alongside single breath count monitoring (a bedside check of respiratory reserve) and physiotherapy for both lower limbs.

Over the following days her backache gradually eased and her fresh complaints didn't recur, but her neurological findings stayed essentially unchanged — power steady at 4-/5 in all four limbs, reflexes and sensation normal, no new deficits. On day two of this documented course, methylprednisolone was added as a single infusion, without a stated response noted afterward; her medication list was otherwise adjusted day to day (analgesics, laxatives, continued physiotherapy). She was discharged after a short stay with her working diagnosis of quadriparesis still framed as "under evaluation" — the specific cause was not resolved in the record available.
